📘 How to Answer Each Question Type

The structure you should follow for every Task 2 essay type

✅ Agree / Disagree

State your position clearly in the introduction. Acknowledge the other side briefly, then argue your view.

Intro: position → Body 1: main reason → Body 2: second reason + counter → Conclusion

⚖️ Discuss Both Views

You must cover both sides fairly. Your opinion should appear in the intro and conclusion (and ideally in one body paragraph).

Intro: both views + opinion → Body 1: view A → Body 2: view B → Conclusion

➕➖ Advantages / Disadvantages

If the question asks "outweigh", you must decide. List both sides, then clearly state which is stronger.

Intro: state which outweighs → Body 1: stronger side → Body 2: weaker side → Conclusion

👍👎 Positive / Negative

Take a position. Support with reasons and examples. If you say "mostly positive", concede one negative clearly.

Intro: position → Body 1: main positives → Body 2: negatives → Conclusion

🔧 Problem / Solution

Identify 2 causes/problems in one body paragraph and 2 solutions in the other. Solutions must link to the problems.

Intro: restate → Body 1: causes → Body 2: solutions → Conclusion

❓ Two-Part Question

You must answer both questions explicitly. Give equal weight to each part.

Intro: address both questions → Body 1: answer Q1 → Body 2: answer Q2 → Conclusion

The complete writing method

Six Task 2 question types: how to plan and write each one

Use the exact instruction in the question to decide what each paragraph must do. These six labels are practical teaching categories; IELTS does not require you to identify a formal “type” before answering.

Start with the task, not a memorised template.

Underline the command words (for example, agree or disagree, discuss both views, outweigh, why, and what can be done). Count how many separate things the examiner asks you to do. Before writing, make a one-line answer to every part of the prompt, then choose body paragraphs that prove those answers.

Practical target: write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. A focused response of roughly 270–310 words is often manageable, but there is no special score bonus for a particular word count. Four paragraphs can work well; five paragraphs may be better when the argument needs an extra body paragraph. The task and clarity of development determine the structure—not a rigid paragraph rule.

01 · Agree / Disagree (Opinion essay)Give a clear position
How to recognise and analyse it

Typical wording: “To what extent do you agree or disagree?” or “Do you agree or disagree?” The examiner is asking for your judgement on one claim. You do not have to give equal space to the opposing view unless doing so helps explain your position.

Example from this question bank:
“Governments should spend money on railways rather than roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?”
Choose your position before drafting

Pick the position you can support with two distinct, relevant reasons:

  • Strongly agree/disagree: both main body paragraphs develop the same overall position.
  • Partly agree: specify exactly which part you accept and which part you reject; keep that distinction consistent.
  • Do not hedge accidentally: a sentence such as “there are advantages and disadvantages” is not itself an answer to how far you agree.
Full paragraph-by-paragraph structure
  1. Introduction — 2 or 3 sentences: paraphrase the claim; state your exact position and, if useful, preview your two reasons.
  2. Body paragraph 1 — first reason: topic sentence stating the reason; explain why/how it supports your view; give one relevant example; link the result back to the claim.
  3. Body paragraph 2 — second reason: develop a different reason. You may briefly acknowledge an opposing point and explain why it does not change your overall judgement.
  4. Conclusion — 1 or 2 sentences: restate the degree to which you agree and summarise the central reasons. Do not introduce a new argument.
Introduction: paraphrase + clear stance → Body 1: reason A + explanation + example → Body 2: reason B (optional counterpoint and response) → Conclusion: direct final judgement.
Model thesis and topic sentences

Thesis: “I largely agree that railways deserve greater public investment because they can reduce transport emissions and move passengers more efficiently, although roads remain necessary for local access.”

Body 1: “The strongest case for prioritising railways is their lower environmental impact per passenger.”

Body 2: “Rail transport can also use fuel and road space more efficiently than large numbers of individual vehicles.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • Your position directly answers the statement.
  • The stance is clear in the introduction and remains consistent.
  • Each body paragraph explains a reason instead of merely naming it.
  • Examples support the reason rather than replace explanation.

Common problem: discussing both sides at length but never making clear how far you agree. This weakens the directness of the response.

02 · Discuss Both Views and Give Your OpinionCover both views + your view
How to recognise and analyse it

Look for “Discuss both views and give your opinion.” There are three obligations: explain View A, explain View B, and give your own position. Merely describing both camps without an opinion leaves part of the task unanswered.

Example from this question bank:
“Some people say History is one of the most important school subjects. Others think that, in today's world, subjects like science and technology are more important than history. Discuss both views and give your opinion.”
Plan the balance

Give each view a fair explanation. Fair coverage does not mean you must agree with both or give identical word counts. Your opinion should be explicit early and supported through the argument. If one side is more convincing, explain why.

Full paragraph-by-paragraph structure
  1. Introduction: paraphrase the debate; identify both positions; state your own view clearly.
  2. Body 1 — View A: explain the reasoning behind the first side; develop its strongest point; provide a relevant example or implication.
  3. Body 2 — View B + your evaluation: explain the second side accurately; show whether and why you find it more persuasive (or how it fits with your position).
  4. Conclusion: summarise the two sides briefly and reaffirm your opinion. Do not leave your view for the first time until the conclusion.
Introduction: both positions + your opinion → Body 1: why supporters hold View A → Body 2: why supporters hold View B + your evaluation → Conclusion: final position.
Model thesis and topic sentences

Thesis: “Although History helps students understand cultural identity and past mistakes, I believe science and technology deserve greater emphasis because they equip learners to respond to current health, environmental and economic challenges.”

Body 1: “Supporters of History argue that it helps students understand how societies developed and why past conflicts occurred.”

Body 2: “By contrast, science and technology provide practical knowledge that is increasingly important in modern careers and public problem-solving.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • Both views are explained, not just mentioned.
  • Your opinion is clear in the introduction and conclusion.
  • Your own judgement is supported by reasoning in the body.
  • You represent the opposing side fairly before evaluating it.

Common problem: writing two separate descriptions and forgetting “give your opinion.” Another is making one view a straw man by explaining it inaccurately.

03 · Advantages / DisadvantagesCheck whether you must weigh them
First, read the exact final sentence

There are two common forms, and they are not identical:

  • “What are the advantages and disadvantages?” Explain both sides. A final judgement may be useful, but the question does not explicitly ask which side is stronger.
  • “Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?” You must compare their relative importance and clearly answer yes, no, or partly.
Example from this question bank:
“The population of some countries includes a relatively large number of young adults, compared with the number of older people. Do the advantages of this situation outweigh the disadvantages?”
Choose a structure that makes the comparison clear

For an “outweigh” question, you can present the weaker side first and the stronger side second, or use the reverse order. What matters is that the thesis and conclusion make the comparison explicit and the body explains why the benefits or drawbacks carry greater weight.

Full structure — for an “outweigh” question
  1. Introduction: paraphrase the situation and state clearly whether advantages outweigh disadvantages.
  2. Body 1 — side you consider weaker: explain its main drawback or benefit fairly; show why it matters, but indicate any limitation if appropriate.
  3. Body 2 — side you consider stronger: develop the most important points and explain why they have greater overall impact. For each point, show consequences or give a specific example.
  4. Conclusion: directly answer “outweigh?” and summarise the basis of the comparison.
Introduction: situation + explicit comparison → Body 1: weaker side → Body 2: stronger side + why it matters more → Conclusion: clear “outweigh” judgement.

For a plain advantages/disadvantages question: Body 1 can cover the main advantages and Body 2 the main disadvantages, followed by a concise summary. Do not force an “outweigh” thesis when the prompt has not asked for one.

Model thesis and topic sentences

Thesis: “Overall, the advantages of a youthful population outweigh its disadvantages because a large working-age group can stimulate productivity and innovation, provided that governments invest in skills and employment.”

Body 1: “One disadvantage of a youth-heavy population is that some sectors may lack experienced professionals and leaders.”

Body 2: “Nevertheless, a large younger workforce can produce greater long-term gains through innovation, entrepreneurship and economic activity.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • You answered the exact question form.
  • Both sides contain explained points, not a bare list.
  • For “outweigh,” your comparison is explicit and reasoned.
  • The body paragraphs do not contradict the thesis.

Common problem: writing one paragraph about each side but never explaining which is more important when the task explicitly asks “outweigh.”

04 · Positive / Negative DevelopmentEvaluate an overall trend
How to recognise and analyse it

Typical wording: “Do you think this is a positive or negative development?” You must evaluate the trend as a whole. It is sensible to acknowledge both benefits and risks, but the reader must be able to identify whether you consider the development positive, negative, or mainly one with some qualification.

Example from this question bank:
“Nowadays, a growing number of people with health problems are trying alternative medicines and treatments instead of visiting their usual doctor. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?”
Do not confuse it with a simple list

The question asks for an evaluation, not merely a catalogue. Decide which effects matter most. Your reasoning should explain the scale, likelihood, duration or importance of the effects. If you choose “mostly negative,” the main argument should support that overall verdict even if you recognise a benefit.

Full structure
  1. Introduction: paraphrase the trend and clearly label it positive, negative or mostly one of the two.
  2. Body 1 — qualification or secondary side: explain a genuine benefit or a less serious concern; do not exaggerate it just to show balance.
  3. Body 2 — main evaluation: develop the more consequential effects that determine your verdict. Explain why these effects carry more weight.
  4. Conclusion: restate your overall evaluation and the main reason for it.
Introduction: describe trend + overall evaluation → Body 1: relevant secondary effects → Body 2: dominant effects that justify the evaluation → Conclusion: final positive/negative judgement.
Model thesis and topic sentences

Thesis (largely negative): “Although some people are attracted to alternative treatments, I regard replacing a regular doctor with unverified remedies as a largely negative development because it may delay appropriate care and expose patients to inadequately tested products.”

Body 1: “Supporters may value alternative treatments because some offer comfort or are perceived as more natural.”

Body 2: “However, the more serious concern is that relying on treatments without reliable evidence can delay diagnosis and effective medical care.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • Your overall judgement is unmistakable.
  • You explain the significance of the effects.
  • Acknowledging the other side does not make your stance vague.
  • The conclusion matches the judgement developed in the body.

Common problem: “There are advantages and disadvantages” without deciding whether the development is positive or negative overall.

05 · Problem / Solution (including causes and measures)Match solutions to problems
Analyse each verb in the prompt

Prompts may ask for problems and solutions, causes and solutions, or reasons and measures. These are related but not interchangeable. If asked “why?”, explain causes. If asked “what problems?”, explain harmful consequences. If asked “what can be done?”, propose feasible actions.

Example from this question bank:
“In spite of the advances made in agriculture, many people around the world still go hungry. Why is this the case? What can be done about this problem?”
Build a cause → solution chain

Plan a clear relationship between each issue and the response to it. For example: disrupted food distribution → protect supply routes and storage; climate-related crop losses → invest in resilient farming and early-warning systems. Avoid listing general wishes such as “governments should do more” without explaining what they should do and how it would help.

Full paragraph-by-paragraph structure
  1. Introduction: paraphrase the situation and signal that you will address the causes/problems and the requested remedies.
  2. Body 1 — causes or problems: identify one or two main points; explain the mechanism behind each and its consequence; use a relevant example where helpful.
  3. Body 2 — solutions: propose practical actions that correspond directly to the causes/problems; identify who should act and explain the expected result.
  4. Conclusion: summarise the key causes/problems and the most relevant measures without adding an entirely new solution.
Introduction: define the issue + roadmap → Body 1: answer “why/what problems?” → Body 2: answer “what can be done?” with linked, feasible measures → Conclusion: summarise.
Model topic sentences

Body 1: “Hunger persists not simply because of limited food production, but also because conflict and climate-related disasters disrupt access to food.”

Body 2: “Governments and international organisations can reduce these risks by protecting food-distribution networks and supporting climate-resilient agriculture.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • Every question in the prompt is answered.
  • Causes are not confused with consequences.
  • Solutions directly address the stated causes/problems.
  • Each proposed action has a plausible explanation of how it would work.

Common problem: giving several possible solutions but not explaining who would implement them or how they address the causes described.

06 · Two-Part Question (Direct questions)Answer every question mark
How to recognise and analyse it

The prompt asks two direct questions, often about different aspects of the same topic. There may be no familiar phrase like “discuss both views.” Write a short answer to each question in your plan. Do not assume the second question always asks for an opinion; it may ask about effects, solutions, reasons or a judgement.

Example from this question bank:
“Nowadays many people choose to be self-employed, rather than to work for a company or organisation. Why might this be the case? What could be the disadvantages of being self-employed?”
Allocate paragraphs to the questions

If the two questions are “why?” and “what disadvantages?”, Body 1 should answer the reasons and Body 2 should answer the disadvantages. If the second question asks whether something is positive or negative, Body 2 must evaluate that instead. The structure follows the actual sub-questions, not a memorised type label.

Full paragraph-by-paragraph structure
  1. Introduction: paraphrase the context and briefly signpost your answers to both questions. A concise position or preview is usually enough.
  2. Body 1 — Question 1: answer the first question directly in the topic sentence; develop the most important reason or point with explanation and example.
  3. Body 2 — Question 2: answer the second question directly; develop a distinct point and its consequences. If a question has several sub-parts, ensure each is explicitly covered.
  4. Conclusion: briefly synthesise the two answers. Do not introduce a third answer or repeat the entire essay.
Introduction: context + brief answers/roadmap → Body 1: direct answer to Question 1 → Body 2: direct answer to Question 2 → Conclusion: concise synthesis of both answers.
Model thesis and topic sentences

Thesis: “People are often drawn to self-employment because it offers greater flexibility and independence; however, it can leave them with unstable income and fewer employment benefits.”

Body 1: “The main reason many people become self-employed is the greater control they gain over their schedules and projects.”

Body 2: “Despite this freedom, self-employed workers may face financial uncertainty and must arrange benefits that an employer would normally provide.”

Band 7+ Task Response check
  • Each question has a visible, direct answer.
  • Neither answer receives only a passing sentence while the other dominates.
  • Each main answer is developed and supported.
  • The body paragraphs clearly correspond to the planned answers.

Common problem: writing an introduction that paraphrases the topic and then discussing it generally, while leaving one of the direct questions unanswered.

How examiners assess the essay

IELTS Writing Task 2 Band Descriptors: practical breakdown

The four criteria apply to all six essay types. Structure helps you answer the task, but a structure by itself does not earn a band score.

Four equally weighted Task 2 criteria

Task Response (TR): did you answer every part, maintain a clear position where required, and develop relevant ideas? Coherence & Cohesion (CC): can the reader follow the logical progression, paragraphing and links between ideas? Lexical Resource (LR): is vocabulary sufficiently varied, accurate and appropriate? Grammatical Range & Accuracy (GRA): do you use a range of sentence structures accurately, with well-controlled grammar and punctuation?

The official IELTS guidance says the four criteria are weighted equally for each task and that Task 2 carries more weight than Task 1 in the overall Writing score. These are paraphrased study notes, not a replacement for the full official descriptors.

1 · Task Response — the first priority

Before submitting, mark every instruction in the question and find the sentence or paragraph that answers it. For opinion tasks, locate your position. For “discuss both views,” locate both views and your own opinion. For “outweigh,” locate the comparison. For two-part prompts, locate both answers. A polished essay that misses one task requirement can still lose marks.

2 · Coherence & Cohesion — reader journey

Each paragraph should have one controlling idea. A topic sentence introduces that idea; the following sentences explain and support it. Use linking words only when they express a real relationship. Pronouns and phrases such as “this policy” or “such an approach” should clearly refer to an idea already mentioned.

3 · Lexical Resource — precise, natural wording

Choose words for meaning, not for impressiveness. Use collocations naturally (for example, “reduce emissions,” “pose a risk,” “allocate funding,” and “address a problem”). Repeated or inaccurately used advanced words do not outperform accurate, topic-appropriate language. Avoid memorised phrases that do not fit the question.

4 · Grammatical Range & Accuracy — controlled variety

Combine accurate simple sentences with well-controlled complex forms, such as subordinate clauses, relative clauses and conditionals. Check subject–verb agreement, articles, plural endings, verb forms, sentence boundaries and punctuation. Do not create complex sentences merely to demonstrate complexity if the grammar becomes unreliable.

How the six question types affect the criteria

Task Response varies most by type: each type has different required content. CC, LR and GRA do not change by type: the same criteria apply to every essay, so logical organisation, suitable vocabulary, and accurate grammatical variety matter throughout.

A body paragraph that develops an idea

Claim → Explain → Example → Link (CEEL): state one answer or reason; explain why/how it is true; illustrate it with a specific and relevant example; then connect its result back to the question or your position. This is a planning aid, not a compulsory formula. Some paragraphs need more explanation and less example, provided the main idea is fully developed.

Weak development: “Railways are good for the environment. They are very useful. For example, many people use them.”

Stronger development: “Railways can reduce the environmental cost of transport because a single train can carry many passengers in one journey. When more commuters use trains instead of separate cars, fewer vehicles may be needed on busy roads, lowering fuel use and congestion. For instance, a city that improves commuter rail services may give workers a practical alternative to driving every day. This makes rail investment a useful part of a broader emissions-reduction strategy.”

Final 60-second checklist

  • I answered every command and every sub-question.
  • My position is explicit wherever the task requires one.
  • Every body paragraph develops one central claim.
  • My explanation makes the logic of each claim clear.
  • Examples are relevant and linked to the point.
  • Paragraphs progress logically; linkers are not mechanically repeated.
  • My vocabulary is accurate and natural, not merely complicated.
  • I checked articles, verb forms, agreement, plural endings and punctuation.
  • I wrote at least 250 words and left time to proofread.

💡

Universal Task 2 principles

  • Word count: write at least 250 words. Around 270–310 can be a practical target, but relevance and development matter more than a fixed number.
  • Paragraphing: use a clear introduction, logically developed body paragraphs and a conclusion. Four paragraphs often work; use another body paragraph when the argument genuinely needs it.
  • Position: state and maintain a clear opinion throughout — do not sit on the fence unless the question allows it.
  • Cohesion: organise ideas logically and use linkers, reference and substitution naturally. Do not add a transition word to every sentence.
  • Development: explain why or how each point supports your answer. A relevant example can help, but an example is not compulsory in every paragraph if the idea is already well developed.
